lines.text: So Dalton takes his question to the experts. Manchester, the last day of October, seventeen ninety-four.
He moved to the town the year before. He's twenty-eight. He teaches mathematics and natural philosophy. That's the old name for the study of nature. And his college is called the New College.

Tonight, he stands up in front of the town's Literary and Philosophical Society and reads out a paper. Its title is "Extraordinary facts relating to the vision of colours". The subject is his own eyes. It's his first paper to the Society.
And it's a careful paper. He doesn't just say that he sees colours oddly. He lists them, one by one, with examples anyone can check.
Here's one. The face of a laurel leaf, he says, is a good match to a stick of red sealing-wax. That's the wax people once used to seal letters.
Think about that. A green leaf and a red stick of wax. To you, about as different as two colours get. To him, a match.

He describes the band of colours from a prism too. A prism is a triangular piece of glass that throws colours on a wall. The part that others call red, he writes, looks to him "little more than a shade, or defect of light". Almost no light at all. Where others see six colours, he sees two, or at most three. Yellow and blue. Or yellow, blue and purple.
Then he does what a scientist should. He offers an explanation.

Your eye isn't hollow. It's filled with clear fluids. The biggest is a clear jelly called the vitreous humour. Here, humour is an old word for a fluid in the body. Light passes through it on its way to the back of the eye.

Dalton's guess is that in his eyes, one of these fluids isn't clear. It's tinted. In his words, "probably some modification of blue". So, some kind of blue. And he supposes it must be the vitreous humour. And honestly?

it makes sense. Think of looking at the world through blue glass. In Dalton's version, the tinted jelly soaks up much of the red and the green light. Before it ever reaches the back of the eye. Reds and greens would both look duller and more like each other. And a red stick of wax might end up looking like a leaf.

He has a reason for picking the jelly, too. "Otherwise," he writes, "I apprehend it might be discovered by inspection, which has not been done." In other words, a tint anywhere easier to see would have been noticed by now.
So the only way to check the jelly is to open an eye. And Dalton only has two.
At some point, he asks for exactly that. For his eyes to be examined after he dies. His biographer would call it his "strongly expressed wish".
But a blue tint only explains colours if we know what colour is. And on that, Dalton leans on one man. A man who died long before Dalton was born.
